chandler.label: Chandler (1987)
chandler.citation: Tertius Chandler, Four Thousand Years of Urban Growth: An Historical Census (1987), as digitized by Reba, Reitsma & Seto, 'Spatializing 6,000 years of global urbanization from 3700 BC to AD 2000', Scientific Data 3, 160034 (2016).
chandler.definition: Built-up urban area including suburbs (Chandler's definition). Pre-modern figures are historians' estimates, not censuses.

wup2018.label: UN WUP 2018
wup2018.citation: United Nations, DESA, Population Division (2018). World Urbanization Prospects: The 2018 Revision, File 22.
wup2018.definition: Urban agglomeration, as each country defines it. Values after the 2018 revision (including 2020 and 2025) are UN projections.

wup2025.label: UN WUP 2025 (Degree of Urbanisation)
wup2025.citation: United Nations, DESA, Population Division (2025). World Urbanization Prospects: The 2025 Revision, File 18.
wup2025.definition: 'City' under the Degree of Urbanisation: a contiguous high-density (1,500+/km²) area of 50,000+ people on a 1 km² grid, applied identically in every country.

wikipedia.label: Wikipedia
wikipedia.citation: English Wikipedia article summaries; images from Wikimedia Commons (individual licences listed per image).

snapshots.label: 1360 BC

cities.name: Thebes
cities.blurb: Egypt's capital at the height of the 18th Dynasty. Amenhotep III built on an unprecedented scale here: the Luxor temple, the Avenue of Sphinxes to Karnak, and on the west bank his vast mortuary temple and the Malkata palace-city.

image.description: The southern Colossus of Memnon (Luxor, Egypt)
image.caption: The southern Colossus of Memnon, one of two giant statues of Amenhotep III at the gateway of his mortuary temple at Thebes; photo 2011.

cities.name: Hattusa
cities.blurb: Hittite capital, with temples in its inner city and a royal acropolis on the Büyükkale ridge. Soon after this date Suppiluliuma I (c. 1344–1322 BC) ringed the inner and outer city with over 6 km of walls.

image.description: Lion Gate, Hattusa, Turkey
image.caption: The Lion Gate in the walls of Hattusa, near Boğazkale, Turkey; photo 2014.

cities.name: Dur-Kurigalzu
cities.blurb: A new royal city founded early in the 14th century BC by the Kassite king Kurigalzu I, who ruled Babylonia from here. It had a ziggurat to Enlil and appeared on toponym lists in Amenhotep III's Egyptian temple.

image.file: 1. The remains of the Kassite ziggurat at Aqar-Quf (Dur-Kurigalzu), western Baghdad, Iraq.jpg
image.description: The remains of the Kassite ziggurat at Aqar-Quf (Dur-Kurigalzu), western Baghdad, Iraq. December 29, 2021.
image.caption: Remains of Kurigalzu's ziggurat at Aqar Quf (Dur-Kurigalzu), west of Baghdad; photo 2021.

cities.name: Ao (Zhengzhou)
cities.blurb: A walled Bronze Age city of the Erligang culture, probably one of the Shang capitals, though which one is uncertain. Rammed-earth walls about 20 m thick at the base enclosed palaces, and bronze-casting workshops lay in the outer city.

image.description: Zhengzhou, Henan Province. Complete indexed photo collection at WorldHistoryPics.com.
image.caption: Surviving stretch of the Shang-dynasty rammed-earth city wall in Zhengzhou; photo 2007.

cities.name: Memphis
cities.blurb: No longer the royal capital, but prosperous: its port, Peru-nefer, was Egypt's gateway to Byblos and the Levant. Amenhotep III built a temple here, 'Nebmaatra united with Ptah', and the first Apis bull burials at Saqqara date from his reign.

image.description: The Sphinx of Memphis in the Memphis open air museum in Egypt.
image.caption: The alabaster Sphinx of Memphis, carved under the 18th Dynasty (probably Amenhotep II or Thutmose IV), in the open-air museum at Mit Rahina; photo 2010.

snapshots.note: Letters found at Amarna record Amenhotep III of Egypt corresponding with the kings of Babylon, Hatti, Assyria and Mitanni, who typically asked him for gold.

snapshots.label: 650 BC

cities.name: Nineveh
cities.blurb: Capital of Ashurbanipal, who built its North Palace and gathered a great library of cuneiform tablets here. Sennacherib had laid out new streets, squares and his 'palace without a rival'. Nineveh was sacked in 612 BC.

image.file: Lion Hunt of Ashurbanipal - king riding killing lion.jpg
image.description: Relief from the lion hunt of king Ashurbanipal. Northern Palace, Nineveh, Room C, c. 645-635 BC. The king, riding a horse, plunges a spear into a lion.
image.caption: Relief from the North Palace at Nineveh showing Ashurbanipal on horseback spearing a lion, carved c. 645–635 BC; British Museum.

cities.name: Luoyang
cities.blurb: Royal seat of the Eastern Zhou, whose court had moved here from Haojing around 770 BC. By now the Zhou kings held little real power over the rival states of the Spring and Autumn period.

image.file: Eastern Zhou Royal Chariot Pit, Luoyang 06.jpg
image.description: Eastern Zhou Chariot Burial and Museum, Luoyang, Henan. Complete indexed photo collection at WorldHistoryPics.com.
image.caption: Excavated Eastern Zhou chariot burial displayed in situ at the Eastern Zhou Royal Chariot Pit museum, Luoyang; photo 2011.

cities.name: Babylon
cities.polity: Babylonia under Shamash-shum-ukin, in revolt against the Neo-Assyrian Empire
cities.blurb: Under siege. Shamash-shum-ukin, the Assyrian prince ruling Babylonia, rebelled against his brother Ashurbanipal in 652 BC. By 650 Assyrian forces were besieging Babylon, which suffered famine and disease before falling in 648.

cities.name: Miletus
cities.blurb: A wealthy Ionian port that, from the seventh century BC, was planting colonies along the Black Sea, such as Sinope and Olbia. It was said to have founded more colonies than any other Greek city.

cities.name: Sais
cities.blurb: Seat of the new Saite dynasty. Psamtik I, who had fled to Nineveh and returned, was recognised as sole king and unified Egypt with Carian and Greek mercenaries sent by Gyges of Lydia.

image.file: LOWTH(1855) - 1.006 RUINS OF SAIS IN THE DELTA.jpg
image.credit: This file is from the Mechanical Curator collection, a set of over 1 million images scanned from out-of-copyright books and released to Flickr Commons by the British Library in London, England. View image on Flickr View all images from book View catalogue entry for book.
image.caption: The ruins of Sais in the Nile Delta, from an illustrated travel book by Lowth published in 1855.

snapshots.note: Assyria shaped much of this list: Ashurbanipal ruled from Nineveh, his army was besieging his rebel brother in Babylon, and Sais's Psamtik I had come to power in Egypt after Assyria drove out the Kushite kings.

snapshots.label: 430 BC

cities.name: Babylon
cities.blurb: Capital of the Persian satrapy of Babylonia and an administrative capital of the Achaemenid Empire, where Babylonian astronomy and mathematics revived. Herodotus described its moat and its huge walls cemented with bitumen.

image.description: Pergamon museum Ishtar Gate in Berlin
image.caption: Nebuchadnezzar's Ishtar Gate of Babylon, rebuilt from excavated glazed bricks in the Pergamon Museum, Berlin; photo 2019.

cities.name: Athens
cities.polity: Athens (city-state, head of the Delian League)
cities.blurb: Pericles had used Delian League tribute to build the Parthenon. Now, in the second year of the war with Sparta, plague spread among refugees crowded inside the Long Walls, killing many, among them soldiers and expert seamen.

image.description: Picture of Parthenon I took in late afternoon.
image.caption: The Parthenon on the Acropolis of Athens seen from the south; photo 2005.

cities.name: Syracuse
cities.blurb: A Corinthian colony founded on the island of Ortygia in 733 BC. Syracuse had fought Akragas and the Sicel leader Ducetius, and its expansion threatened Athenian interests, which would later draw a great Athenian expedition against it.

image.description: Temple of Apollo in Doric order, architect Epikles, ca 565 BC. Piazza Pancali, Ortigia.
image.caption: Remains of the Doric Temple of Apollo on Ortygia, built around 565 BC; photo 2012.

cities.name: Luoyang
cities.blurb: Still the Zhou royal capital, which had moved in 510 BC from Wangcheng to nearby Chengzhou. The Warring States period had just begun, and real power lay with the rival states.

image.file: Eastern Zhou Royal Chariot Pit, Luoyang 07.jpg
image.description: Eastern Zhou Chariot Burial and Museum, Luoyang, Henan. Complete indexed photo collection at WorldHistoryPics.com.
image.caption: Eastern Zhou chariot and horse burial excavated in Luoyang, displayed at the Eastern Zhou Royal Chariot Pit museum; photo 2011.

cities.name: Pataliputra
cities.blurb: Magadha's new capital on the Ganges. King Ajatashatru had fortified the village of Pataligrama, and his son Udayin founded the city where the Son meets the Ganges, moving the capital here from Rajgriha.

cities.name: Memphis
cities.blurb: Capital of Persian-ruled Egypt since Cambyses took it in 525 BC. A permanent Persian garrison held the city near the palace of Apries, and Herodotus visited and described its monuments in this century.

image.file: Relief from the Palace of Apries in Memphis MET DT257081.jpg
image.credit: This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art. See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy
image.description: Relief, wall, Apries
image.date: 589–570 B.C. Period: Late Period, Saite Dynasty: Dynasty 26 Reign: reign of Apries
image.caption: Carved wall relief from the palace of Apries at Memphis, made 589–570 BC; Metropolitan Museum of Art.

snapshots.note: Athens and Sparta had been at war since 431 BC. Syracuse, also on this list, would later be the target of Athens's disastrous Sicilian Expedition.

snapshots.label: 200 BC

cities.name: Chang'an
cities.blurb: A brand-new capital. Liu Bang settled his court here in 202 BC, building Changle Palace across the river from the ruined Qin capital, and two years later the vast Weiyang Palace. Work on the city walls started in 194 BC.

image.description: ​汉长安城遗址之1号建筑-未央宫前殿遗址。
image.caption: Rammed-earth platform of the front hall of Weiyang Palace at the Han Chang'an city site, Xi'an; photo 2013.

cities.name: Pataliputra
cities.blurb: Capital of the Maurya Empire in its last decades. The Greek envoy Megasthenes had described a long city beside the Ganges, ringed by a deep moat and a timber wall with 570 towers and 64 gates.

image.file: Mauryan ruins of pillared hall at Kumrahar site of Pataliputra ASIEC 1912-13.jpg
image.credit: 1912-1913 Archaelogical excavations by ASIEC in Pataliputra [1]
image.description: Mauryan ruins of pillared hall at Kumrahar site of Pataliputra ASIEC 1912-13
image.caption: Excavated remains of a Mauryan pillared hall at Kumhrar, Pataliputra, photographed for the Archaeological Survey of India in 1912–13.

cities.name: Alexandria
cities.blurb: Capital of Ptolemaic Egypt, known for its Pharos lighthouse and its Great Library. Around 200 BC Aristophanes of Byzantium became the Library's fourth head, after Eratosthenes, who had calculated the Earth's circumference.

image.description: A drawing of the Pharos of Alexandria by German archaeologist Prof. H. Thiersch (1909).
image.caption: Reconstruction drawing of the Pharos lighthouse of Alexandria by the archaeologist Hermann Thiersch, 1909.

cities.name: Seleucia
cities.blurb: Founded around 305 BC by Seleucus I as his first capital, largely peopled from Babylon. The court later moved to Antioch, but Seleucia, on the Tigris and a Euphrates canal, remained one of the great Hellenistic cities.

cities.correction: Missing from the digitized set for 200 BC. Chandler (1987) gives Rome 150,000-160,000 at 200 BC, as cited on Wikipedia 'Historical urban community sizes' (Table 2). Lower bound used.
cities.name: Rome
cities.blurb: Just victorious over Carthage, Rome was for the first time the capital of an overseas empire. From the 2nd century BC its population surged as Italian farmers, pushed off the land by slave-run estates, moved to the city.

image.artist: No machine-readable author provided. Joris assumed (based on copyright claims).
image.credit: No machine-readable source provided. Own work assumed (based on copyright claims).
image.description: Servian Wall, near Stazione Termini, Rome, Italy.
image.caption: Surviving section of the Servian Wall, Rome's early 4th-century BC city wall, beside Termini station; photo 2005.

cities.name: Carthage
cities.blurb: Defeated at Zama in 202 BC, Carthage accepted Roman peace terms that stripped its overseas territories and imposed a heavy indemnity. A grid-planned residential quarter on the Byrsa hill dates from about this time.

image.file: Punic Ports (Ports Puniques) of Carthage, Tunisia January 2024 - 1.jpg
image.description: 36.84484° N, 10.32386° E, Site Archéologique de Carthage
image.caption: The site of Carthage's Punic ports, the city's two artificial inner harbours; photo 2024.

snapshots.note: Two new orders had just emerged: Rome ended the Second Punic War victorious over Carthage in 201 BC, and in 202 BC Liu Bang founded the Han dynasty and made Chang'an its capital.
caveats: The digitized Chandler dataset (Reba et al. 2016) lists Chang'an at 400,000 in 200 BC, but Wikipedia's transcription of Chandler (1987) names Pataliputra (350,000) as the largest city that year. Chang'an only became the Han capital in 202 BC, so treat its ranking this year with caution. Not resolved without the book itself.

snapshots.label: AD 361

cities.correction: Missing from the digitized set for AD 361. Chandler (1987) names Constantinople the largest city in 361 at 300,000, per Wikipedia 'List of largest cities throughout history' (Chandler column).
cities.name: Constantinople
cities.blurb: Constantine's city, proclaimed the new capital of the Roman Empire in 330. His son Constantius II, who took the eastern provinces including Constantinople, died in November 361 on the brink of civil war with his cousin Julian.

image.description: Column of Constantine, Istanbul
image.caption: The Column of Constantine, completed around 328 for the city's dedication and still standing in Istanbul's Çemberlitaş district; photo 2018.

cities.name: Ctesiphon
cities.blurb: Capital of Shapur II, who renewed war on Rome in 359 and retook Singara and Amida. In 363 the emperor Julian would defeat Shapur's forces outside Ctesiphon but fail to take the city.

image.description: Palacio de Ctesifonte
image.caption: The Taq Kasra, the great arched hall of Ctesiphon's royal palace, drawn in 1824; its construction date, somewhere between the 3rd and 6th centuries, is disputed.

cities.name: Antioch
cities.blurb: Seat of the count of the East and a mixed pagan and Christian city, whose leading church was Constantine's Great Church, begun in 327. The next year Julian, on campaign against Persia, would clash bitterly with its citizens.

image.description: Part of the border of the Megalopsychia hunt mosaic from the latter half of the 5th century from Daphne (Yakto) that may show the Imperial Palace and Great Church of Antioch
image.caption: Detail from the border of the late 5th-century Megalopsychia mosaic from Daphne, thought to show Antioch's imperial palace and Great Church.

cities.name: Rome
cities.blurb: Still formally a capital, but emperors now ruled from elsewhere. Rome kept its prestige: Constantine had given the Lateran Palace to the Pope and built Old St Peter's, while its senators remained a stronghold of paganism.

image.description: Arch of Constantine (Rome) ,lateral view
image.caption: The Arch of Constantine, erected to celebrate his victory over Maxentius; photo 2014.

cities.name: Pataliputra
cities.blurb: Re-emerging as an important city under the Gupta dynasty, whose reputed capital it was, though historians debate this. The reigning king, Samudragupta, is praised on the Allahabad Pillar for wide conquests and as a poet and musician.

cities.name: Jiankang
cities.blurb: Capital of the Eastern Jin since 317, when Sima Rui made it his seat after northern China fell. Its palaces were rebuilt in 330–332, setting the city's layout, though it still had only bamboo stockades, not brick walls.

image.file: 20240604 Site of Jiankang in the Oriental Metropolitan Museum.jpg
image.description: Excavation site of Jiankang in the Oriental Metropolitan Museum
image.caption: Excavated remains of Six Dynasties Jiankang displayed in the Oriental Metropolitan Museum, Nanjing; photo 2024.

snapshots.note: The two largest cities were rival capitals: Rome's war with Shapur II's Sasanian Empire had flared again in 359, and Constantius II went east in 360 after losing border fortresses.

snapshots.label: AD 500

cities.name: Constantinople
cities.blurb: Capital of the Eastern Roman Empire, which flourished while the western half collapsed. The double line of the Theodosian Walls, built this century, now protected it, and for most of the Byzantine period it was Europe's largest city.

image.description: Theodosian Walls of Constantinople, Istanbul
image.caption: A surviving stretch of the 5th-century Theodosian Walls of Constantinople, Istanbul; photo 2017.

cities.name: Ctesiphon
cities.blurb: Kavad I had just regained his throne, returning to the capital in 498 with a Hephthalite army after nobles deposed him for backing Mazdak's egalitarian sect. Veh-Ardashir, the western district, was seat of the Nestorian patriarch.

image.artist: Unknown authorUnknown author (American Colony Photo Department)
image.credit: This image is available from the United States Library of Congress's Prints and Photographs division under the digital ID matpc.13139.This tag does not indicate the copyright status of the attached work. A normal copyright tag is still required. See Commons:Licensing.
image.description: Ruins of Ctesiphon
image.caption: The ruined Taq Kasra palace arch at Ctesiphon, photographed in 1932; the arch dates from sometime between the 3rd and 6th centuries.

cities.name: Luoyang
cities.blurb: Emperor Xiaowen of Northern Wei moved his capital here in 493 as part of his sinicization campaign. Work began on the Buddhist Longmen Grottoes, and the Yongning Temple pagoda, China's tallest, was built in the city.

image.description: Longmen Grottoes in Luoyang, China
image.caption: Cliffside Buddhist caves of the Longmen Grottoes near Luoyang, begun under the Northern Wei; photo 2019.

cities.name: Jiankang
cities.blurb: Capital of the Southern Qi. The city gained brick walls around 480 and hosted literary circles such as the Eight Friends of Jingling. Rebellions against Emperor Xiao Baojuan would soon bring Xiao Yan's Liang dynasty to power.

image.description: Plan schématique de Jiankang sous les dynasties du Sud, d'après les textes de l'époque. A partir de Albert E. Dien, Six Dynasties Civilization, New Haven, Yale University Press, coll. « Early Chinese civilization series », 2007, p. 37-45 et Nancy S. Steinhardt (dir.) et Fu Xinian, Guo Daiheng, Liu Xujie, Pan Guxi, Qiao Yun, Sun Dazhang, L'Architecture chinoise, Arles, Philippe Picquier, 2005, p. 67.
image.caption: Schematic plan of Jiankang under the Southern Dynasties, drawn in 2016 from period texts and modern studies.

cities.name: Antioch
cities.blurb: A great Eastern Roman city, still centred on Constantine's Great Church. In 490 or 491 riots led by the Green circus faction turned on its Jews. Earthquakes in 526 and 528 would soon devastate it.

image.file: The Megalopsychia Hunt of Antioch mosaic, late 5th century AD, found in the village of Yakto near Daphne, Hatay Archaeology Museum, Antakya, Turke - 50735694481.jpg
image.description: The Megalopsychia Hunt of Antioch mosaic, late 5th century AD, found in the village of Yakto near Daphne, Hatay Archaeology Museum, Antakya, Turke - 50735694481
image.caption: The Megalopsychia Hunt mosaic, made in the late 5th century and found at Yakto near Daphne, whose border is thought to show buildings of Antioch; Hatay Archaeology Museum.

snapshots.note: The last Western Roman emperor had been deposed in 476, leaving Constantinople as the surviving Roman capital. China was split between the Northern Wei, ruling from Luoyang, and southern dynasties at Jiankang.

snapshots.label: AD 622

cities.name: Ctesiphon
cities.blurb: Capital of Khosrow II's Sasanian Empire, a sprawling metropolis of several districts known in Arabic as al-Mada'in. In 627 the Byzantine emperor Heraclius would surround the city before the Persians accepted his peace terms.

image.description: Taq Kasra - 1934
image.caption: The Taq Kasra arch, once part of the Sasanian royal palace at Ctesiphon, photographed in 1934.

cities.name: Chang'an
cities.blurb: Only four years earlier Li Yuan had proclaimed the Tang dynasty here, renaming the Sui capital Daxing, laid out from 582 on a grid of walled wards, as Chang'an.

image.file: 2023-10-07 Model of Chang'an City of the Tang Dynasty 唐代長安城模型.jpg
image.description: Model of Chang'an City of the Tang Dynasty
image.caption: Modern scale model of Tang-dynasty Chang'an, photographed in 2023.

cities.name: Constantinople
cities.blurb: Heraclius's capital was under pressure: Persian conquests had cut its Egyptian grain supply, ending free bread in 618, and Avars threatened from the Balkans. In 626 it would withstand a joint Sasanian–Avar siege.

image.description: Theodosian Walls of Constantinople, Istanbul
image.caption: Surviving stretch of the Theodosian land walls of Constantinople, photographed in 2017.

cities.name: Luoyang
cities.blurb: Rebuilt from 604 by Sui Emperor Yang on a plan inspired by his father's Chang'an. In June 621 the warlord Wang Shichong surrendered it to the Tang prince Li Shimin after a long siege.

image.description: Site of Dingding Gate
image.caption: Excavated site of Dingding Gate of Sui–Tang Luoyang, photographed in 2025.

cities.name: Kannauj
cities.blurb: Imperial capital of Harsha, who united much of northern India after 606. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, visiting during his reign, described a large, prosperous city with many Buddhist monasteries.

image.credit: CNG Coins Coin from CNG coins. Used with permission (CNG coin [1]). Coin [2]
image.description: Harshavardhana Circa AD 606-647. AR Drachm (13mm, 2.28 g, 1h). Head left; crescent above / Fan-tailed Garuda standing facing.
image.caption: Silver drachm of Harshavardhana, struck during his reign (606–647).

snapshots.note: Ctesiphon and Constantinople were locked in the last and most devastating Roman–Persian war; Heraclius's counter-attacks began in 622, and in the 630s Arab armies invaded both exhausted empires.

snapshots.label: AD 800

cities.name: Baghdad
cities.blurb: Founded in 762 by Caliph al-Mansur around his walled Round City, the Abbasid capital had within a generation become a hub of learning and commerce on the Tigris trade routes.

image.file: Round City in the Time of Mansur (Le Strange).png
image.credit: Guy Le Strange (1900). Baghdad During the Abbasid Caliphate from Contemporary Arabic and Persian Sources. Oxford: Clarendon Press, Map II.

Quadrangle of Shabib
image.caption: Guy Le Strange's plan of al-Mansur's Round City of Baghdad, published in 1900.

cities.name: Chang'an
cities.blurb: The Tang capital was recovering after rebels in 756 and Tibetans in 763 occupied it. Sogdian, Indian and Arab residents lived here, and the city had Zoroastrian temples and a Church of the East church.

image.file: Reconstruction Model of Hanyuan Hall of Daming Palace.jpg
image.description: CG restoration of Hanyuan Hall in Daming Palace in the Tang Dynasty
image.caption: Computer reconstruction of Hanyuan Hall in the Tang Daming Palace at Chang'an, made in 2016.

cities.name: Luoyang
cities.blurb: The Tang 'Eastern Capital' (Dongdu), damaged in the An Lushan Rebellion. Early 9th-century epitaphs record Christian Sogdian women and their Han Chinese husbands living here.

image.description: Fengxian Temple‎ at Luoyang in China
image.caption: Fengxian Temple at the Longmen Grottoes south of Luoyang, where most caves date from the Northern Wei and Tang; photographed in 2012.

cities.name: Constantinople
cities.blurb: Empress Irene ruled alone from here after blinding her son in 797, an empress reigning in her own right. On Christmas Day 800, Charlemagne's coronation as emperor in Rome challenged her claim.

image.description: Irene. 797-802. Solidus (Gold, 18mm, 4.43 g 6), Constantinople. ϵIRInH bASILISSH Bust of Irene facing, wearing loros and crown with cross, pinnacles and pendilia, holding a globus cruciger in her right hand and a cross tipped scepter in her left. Rev. ϵIRInH bASILISSHΘ Bust of Irene facing, wearing loros and crown with cross, pinnacles and pendilia, holding a globus cruciger in her right hand and a cross tipped scepter in her left.
image.caption: Gold solidus of Empress Irene, struck at Constantinople during her sole reign (797–802).

cities.name: Heian-kyō
cities.blurb: Emperor Kanmu entered his new capital in 794, a grid city modelled on Tang Chang'an. Construction was still under way; the palace-building office closed only in 805.

image.credit: Own work PENTAX K-1 + smc PENTAX-A 1:2.8 20mm
image.description: Over all model of Heian-kyō
image.caption: Modern scale model of the planned capital Heian-kyō, photographed in 2018.

snapshots.note: Tang Chang'an, Abbasid Baghdad and Byzantine Constantinople, three imperial capitals, were among the largest cities in the world.

cities.name: Córdoba
cities.blurb: The Umayyad capital was ruled in practice by the chamberlain Almanzor, with Caliph Hisham II a figurehead. Within a decade civil war broke out, and Berber troops sacked the city in 1013.

image.description: Maqsura y Mihrab de la Mezquita de Córdoba (España).
image.caption: Maqsura and mihrab of the Great Mosque of Córdoba, added in al-Hakam II's expansion from 962; photographed in 2011.

cities.name: Kaifeng
cities.blurb: The Northern Song had made this canal city their Eastern Capital (Dongjing) in 960. An outer city added in 955 enclosed a growing commercial centre where four major canals met.

image.description: Po Pagoda in Kaifeng
image.caption: Po Pagoda in Kaifeng, a Song-dynasty pagoda dating from 974, now partly destroyed; photographed in 2018.

cities.name: Constantinople
cities.blurb: Basil II ruled from here, guarded since 980 by the Varangian Guard, warriors sent by Prince Vladimir of Kiev. The city's trades were organised into guilds supervised by the Eparch.

image.artist: Authors of Menologion of Basil II (circa 985 AC, Constantinople), Byzantine manuscript illuminators[1]: Pantoleon with Georgios, Michael the Younger, Michael of Blachernae, Symeon, Symeon of Blachernae, Menas, and Nestor (Online on Vatican site)
image.description: Menologion of Basil II. Christmas
image.caption: Nativity page from the Menologion of Basil II, an illuminated manuscript compiled at Constantinople around 1000.

cities.name: Angkor
cities.blurb: The Khmer capital Yasodharapura, built by Yasovarman around the Phnom Bakheng temple and a great reservoir. Around 1002 Suryavarman I seized power, fighting a nine-year succession war.

image.description: Phnom Bakheng in Angkor, Cambodia
image.caption: Phnom Bakheng, the late 9th-century temple-mountain at the centre of Yasovarman's city; photographed in 2008.

cities.name: Heian-kyō
cities.blurb: The Heian capital's life had shifted to its northern and eastern districts as the western Right Capital declined. Its great southern gate, Rajōmon, had collapsed in a storm in 980 and was never rebuilt.

image.description: Miniature Model of Heiankyo Rajomon. 平安京羅城門復元模型（京都文化博物館）
image.caption: Modern miniature model of Rajōmon, Heian-kyō's southern gate, at the Museum of Kyoto.

caveats: The digitized dataset gives Córdoba 450,000 in 1000, the figure widely quoted from Chandler; Wikipedia's list of largest cities gives Chandler's figure as 350,000. Either way it is Chandler's largest city that year.

cities.name: Kaifeng
cities.blurb: The Northern Song capital at its peak had night markets, theatres, the Iron Pagoda of 1049 and Su Song's water-driven astronomical clock tower. Jurchen invaders would take the city in 1127.

image.description: part of the Qingming Scroll (清明上河圖 qīng míng shàng hé tú) by the Song-Dynasty Chinese painter Zhang Zeduan (張擇端; Simplified Chinese: 张择端; Hanyu Pinyin: Zhāng Zéduān)
image.caption: Detail of Along the River During the Qingming Festival, the Northern Song painter Zhang Zeduan's (1085–1145) scroll of the capital.

cities.name: Constantinople
cities.blurb: Under Alexios I Komnenos the empire was recovering. The Pechenegs had reached the walls in 1090–91 and been destroyed, and in 1096 the First Crusade assembled here before marching on Jerusalem.

image.description: Topographical map of Constantinople during the Byzantine period.
image.caption: Modern topographical map of Constantinople in the Byzantine period, drawn in 2008.

cities.name: Marrakesh
cities.blurb: Founded around 1070 as the Almoravid capital, the young city ruled an emirate stretching from Senegal to central Spain. Its fortified palace and the square before its gates became the core of later Marrakesh.

image.description: Almoravid Qubba in Marrakesh (view from south)
image.caption: The Almoravid Qubba, a rare surviving Almoravid building erected in the early 12th century; photographed in 2023.

cities.name: Baghdad
cities.blurb: Since Tughril Beg took the city in 1055, Seljuk sultans ruled in the name of the Abbasid caliphs. Their vizier Nizam al-Mulk had founded the Nizamiyya college here.

cities.name: Kalyani (Basavakalyan)
cities.blurb: Royal capital of the Western Chalukyas since about 1042. King Vikramaditya VI, who beat the Cholas at Vengi in 1093, kept the poet Bilhana and the jurist Vijnaneshwara, author of the Mitakshara, at court.

cities.name: Cairo
cities.blurb: The Fatimid palace-city was opening up after vizier Badr al-Gamali let wealthy families from Fustat move in. Between 1087 and 1092 he rebuilt its walls in stone with the gates Bab al-Futuh, Bab al-Nasr and Bab Zuweila.

image.description: Cairo, Egypt: the medieval city gate Bab al-Futuh: with joggling above a doorway[1]
image.caption: Bab al-Futuh, one of the stone gates built by Badr al-Gamali between 1087 and 1092; photographed in 2019.

caveats: Heian-kyō (Kyoto) is not recorded for 1100 in the digitized dataset. Chandler has it at 175,000 in 1000 and 150,000 in 1150, so it probably belongs in this year's top 5 (tied around 150,000).

cities.name: Hangzhou
cities.blurb: As Lin'an, capital of the Southern Song since 1132, after the Jurchens took Kaifeng. Crowded with northern refugees, it spread far beyond its old ramparts, and in 1208 a four-day fire burned tens of thousands of houses.

image.file: Leifeng Pagoda in the Southern Song Dynasty by Li Song.jpg
image.description: 南宋李嵩《西湖图》局部，示雷峰塔南宋时的形象
image.caption: Leifeng Pagoda by West Lake, detail of a West Lake painting by the Southern Song artist Li Song (13th century).

cities.name: Cairo
cities.blurb: Saladin's Citadel, begun in 1176, and a new wall linking Cairo with Fustat were being completed by his Ayyubid successors. The former Fatimid palace-city was opening to ordinary Egyptians and foreign merchants.

image.file: The massive walls of the Cairo Citadel (14815621603).jpg
image.credit: The massive walls of the Cairo Citadel
image.description: The Saladin Citadel of Cairo is a medieval Islamic fortification in Cairo, Egypt. The location, on Mokattam hill near the center of Cairo, was once famous for its fresh breeze and grand views of the city. It is now a preserved historic site, with mosques and museums. The Citadel was fortified by the Ayyubid ruler Salah al-Din (Saladin) between 1176 and 1183 CE, to protect it from the Crusaders. Only a few years after defeating the Fatimid Caliphate, Saladin set out to build a wall that would surround both Cairo and Fustat. Saladin is recorded as saying, "With a wall I will make the two [cities of Cairo and Fustat] into a unique whole, so that one army may defend them both; and I believe it is good to encircle them with a single wall from the bank of the Nile to the bank of the Nile." The Citadel would be the centerpiece of the wall. Built on a promontory beneath the Muqattam Hills, a setting that made it difficult to attack, the efficacy of the Citadel's location is further demonstrated by the fact that it remained the heart of Egyptian government until the 19th century. The citadel stopped being the seat of government when Egypt's ruler, Khedive Ismail, moved to his newly built Abdin Palace in the Ismailiya neighborhood in the 1860s. While the Citadel was completed in 1183–1184, the wall Saladin had envisioned was still under construction in 1238, long after his death [Wikipedia.org]
image.caption: Walls of Saladin's Citadel of Cairo, begun in 1176; photographed in 2012.

cities.name: Fez
cities.blurb: After fierce resistance, the Almohads took Fez in 1145 and tore down its walls. The new ramparts ordered by Ya'qub al-Mansur were completed in 1204 and still mark the perimeter of Fes el-Bali.

image.description: Bab Mahrouk, Fes. Built in 1204.
image.caption: Bab Mahrouk, the western gate of Fes el-Bali, built in 1204; photographed in 2014.

cities.name: Pagan (Bagan)
cities.blurb: Capital of the Pagan Kingdom at its zenith under King Narapatisithu, who built the Sulamani Temple in 1183. The half-century to 1200 was the peak of monument building on the Bagan plain.

image.description: Sulamani Temple is a Buddhist temple located in Bagan (Pagan), in Burma/Myanmar, built in 1183 by King Narapatisithu.
image.caption: Sulamani Temple, built by King Narapatisithu in 1183; photographed in 2008.

cities.name: Kamakura
cities.blurb: Seat of the warrior government Minamoto no Yoritomo set up here in 1180. After he died in 1199, his teenage son Yoriie succeeded under the regency of Hōjō Tokimasa, and real power began passing to the Hōjō.

cities.name: Hangzhou
cities.blurb: The former Song capital was taken, but spared, by Kublai Khan's armies in 1276, and remained an important southern commercial and administrative centre. Marco Polo supposedly visited and called it greater than any city in the world.

cities.name: Khanbaliq
cities.blurb: Kublai Khan's planned capital, laid out from 1264 around Jade Island following the Confucian Rites of Zhou and completed only in 1293. Buddhists, Muslims, Christians, Taoists and Confucians all had houses of worship here.

image.description: Karta över Zhongdu och Dadu
image.caption: Modern map showing the extent of Yuan Dadu and the earlier Jin capital Zhongdu, drawn in 2015.

cities.name: Cairo
cities.blurb: The Mamluks, who had repelled the Mongols and ended the Crusader states, were filling the old palace district with religious complexes. Under Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, Cairo was approaching its peak of wealth.

image.description: Qalawun complex in Islamic Cairo, Egypt
image.caption: The Qalawun complex, built by Sultan Qalawun in 1284–1285, photographed in 2024.

cities.name: Paris
cities.blurb: Philip IV was rebuilding the royal residence on the Île de la Cité as a palace. On the Left Bank, the Latin Quarter's university was Western Europe's leading school of Catholic theology.

image.file: Vie de Saint Denis - BNF Fr2092 37v.jpg
image.caption: Bridges of Paris with wheat mills, a miniature from the Life of St Denis made around 1317.

cities.name: Kamakura
cities.blurb: Seat of the Hōjō regency, which gave the city great temples such as Kenchō-ji and Engaku-ji. It was recovering from a severe earthquake in 1293; the regency would fall at the Siege of Kamakura in 1333.

image.file: The Great Buddha of Kōtoku-in (Kamakura Daibutsu).jpg
image.description: The Great Buddha of Kōtoku-in (The Great Buddha of Kamakura), Kōtoku-in, Kamakura, Kanagawa Prefecture, Japan The Great Buddha of Kamakura, also known as The Great Buddha of Kōtoku-in. (鎌倉大仏, Kamakura Daibutsu) is a bronze statue of Amida Buddha, which stands on the grounds of Kōtoku-in. This 11.4-meter high statue has long been the second tallest bronze Buddha statue in Japan, surpassed only by the statue at Todai-ji in Nara.
image.caption: The bronze Great Buddha of Kōtoku-in, dating from around 1252; photographed in 2021.

cities.name: Nanjing
cities.blurb: Ming capital since 1368, Nanjing was ringed by a Capital City wall more than 30 km long. In 1400 the Jianwen Emperor ruled here while at war with his uncle Zhu Di, who would seize the city in 1402.

image.description: The Zhonghua Gate complex at the southern part of the City Wall of Nanjing
image.caption: The Zhonghua Gate complex on the southern side of the Nanjing city wall, photographed in 2008.

cities.name: Vijayanagara
cities.blurb: On the banks of the Tungabhadra River, Vijayanagara was capital of an empire that Harihara II (r. 1377–1404) had consolidated beyond the Krishna River, bringing South India under its control.

image.file: Ruins of Vijianuggur, the market in front of Virupaksha temple also called Hampi bazaar, Hampi, Vijayanagara, 1868 photo.jpg
image.description: Photographer: Lyon, Edmund David Medium: Photographic print Year created: 1868 Year published: 1868 Collection Photo 212/7(14) now at the British Library Vijayanagara, the City of Victory, was the most powerful Hindu kingdom in Southern India from 1336 until 1565. It was founded on the bank of the Tungabhadra River by two brothers, Harihara and Bukka, formerly chieftains with the Delhi Sultanate. Vijayanagara flourished as a prosperous centre of Hindu art, culture and architecture, until the Battle of Talikota in 1565 when it was defeated by the armies of a coalition of neighbouring Muslim kingdoms.
image.caption: The ruined bazaar street in front of the Virupaksha temple at Hampi, photographed by Edmund David Lyon in 1868.

cities.name: Cairo
cities.blurb: Capital of the Mamluk Sultanate, now ruled by the Burji Mamluks, Cairo was still reeling from repeated plague and political instability since 1348. The era had nonetheless produced the Madrasa-Mosque of Sultan Hasan, the largest Mamluk-era religious monument.

image.description: Mosque of Sultan Hasan, Cairo, Egypt.
image.caption: The Madrasa-Mosque of Sultan Hasan, the largest Mamluk-era religious monument in Cairo, photographed in 2012.

cities.name: Paris
cities.blurb: Paris lay inside the new wall Charles V had built between 1356 and 1383, guarded by his Bastille fortress. But plague kept returning and the Hundred Years' War dragged on; the English would take the city in 1420.

image.file: Les Très Riches Heures du duc de Berry octobre.jpg
image.description: La scène paysanne du premier plan représente les semailles. À droite, un homme sème à la volée. Des pies et des corneilles picorent les graines qui viennent d'être semées, à proximité d'un sac blanc et d'une gibecière. Derrière, un épouvantail en forme d'archer et des fils tendus, sur lesquels sont accrochés des plumes, sont destinés à éloigner les oiseaux. À gauche, un paysan à cheval passe la herse sur laquelle est posée une pierre qui permet aux dents de pénétrer plus profondément dans la terre. Il recouvre ainsi les grains qui viennent d'être semés. À l'arrière-plan, le peintre a représenté le Palais du Louvre. Du château au centre, on distingue, outre le donjon central qui accueillait alors le trésor royal, la façade orientale à droite, encadrée par la tour de la Taillerie et la tour de la Chapelle, et à gauche la façade méridionale, avec ses deux tours jumelées au centre. L'ensemble est entouré d'une enceinte ponctuée de trois tours et de deux bretèches, visibles ici. Sur la rive, des personnages conversent ou se promènent.
image.caption: October page of the Très Riches Heures du duc de Berry, painted between 1412 and 1416, with the Louvre fortress behind the Seine.

cities.name: Hangzhou
cities.blurb: The former Southern Song capital, at the southern end of the Grand Canal, was slowly regaining its prosperity under the Ming. Its West Lake, neglected under the Mongols and partly turned into farmland, still awaited restoration.

image.description: Su Causeway
image.caption: The Su Causeway across West Lake, built from dredged silt in 1089, photographed in 2011.

cities.name: Beijing
cities.blurb: Ming capital since 1421, Beijing centred on the Forbidden City, built 1406–1420. Imperial granaries near the Grand Canal's terminus fed its people, who had switched to coal once the surrounding forests were cut down.

image.caption: Detail of the Beijing Palace City Scroll, painted in the mid-Ming dynasty (c. 15th century), showing the Forbidden City.

cities.name: Vijayanagara
cities.blurb: By 1500 Vijayanagara was probably India's richest city, drawing traders from Persia and Portugal. Power lay with the regent Tuluva Narasa Nayaka, who defended the empire against the Gajapati king and the Bahmani Sultan.

image.description: Vijaya Vitthala Temple, Hampi, Karnataka, India, reflected in a shallow pool filled with rainwater. The Vitthala temple and market complex is over 3 kilometres (1.9 miles) north-east of the Virupaksha temple near the banks of the Tungabhadra River. It is an artistically sophisticated Hindu temple in Hampi, and is part of the sacred centre of Vijayanagara.
image.caption: The Vitthala temple complex in the ruins of Vijayanagara at Hampi, photographed in 2019.

cities.name: Cairo
cities.blurb: Sultan Qaytbay (r. 1468–1496) had built or restored numerous monuments in Cairo, but after him the crisis of Mamluk power deepened, and a new sea route around Africa soon let spice traders bypass the city.

image.description: View of Sultan Qaytbay's mosque and mausoleum complex in the Northern Cemetery.
image.caption: Sultan Qaytbay's mosque and mausoleum complex in Cairo's Northern Cemetery, photographed in 2012.

cities.name: Hangzhou
cities.blurb: Hangzhou's harbour was slowly silting up, and the city acted as a feeder to the larger Suzhou market along the Grand Canal. In 1508 governor Yang Mengying would dredge West Lake, repairing its causeways and adding a new one.

image.credit: A Record of Travels at West Lake (Xihu Youlan Zhi), Vol. I, although presumably a later reprint of the Siku Quanshu edition.

image.date: 1547 originally, although presumably a later reprint
image.caption: Map of Hangzhou's prefectural seat under the Ming dynasty, originally made in 1547.

cities.name: Tabriz
cities.blurb: Capital of the Aq Qoyunlu since 1469, Tabriz kept monuments of its earlier Qara Qoyunlu rulers, including the Blue Mosque. In 1501 Ismail I would enter the city and proclaim it capital of his new Safavid state.

image.caption: The Blue Mosque of Tabriz, built in 1465, photographed in the mid-19th century.

cities.name: Beijing
cities.blurb: Beijing now had an Outer City wall, added in 1553 after a Mongol raid. In 1601 the Jesuit Matteo Ricci became an adviser to the Wanli Emperor and the first Westerner admitted to the Forbidden City.

image.description: "Departure Herald", 26 m (85 ft) in length, from the Jiajing reign period (1522-1566 AD); the painting shows the emperor's large procession heading towards the imperial tombs of the Ming emperors located roughly 50 km north of the capital Beijing. This painting is usually paired with another panoramic painting called "Return Clearing", 31 m (98 ft) in length, which shows the emperor returning to the capital from the tombs by river boat. From Paludan's source listed below, this passage describes a particular scene of this painting: "Detail of a silk scroll, The Emperor's Approach, showing the luxury in which the emperor Xuande travelled. Elephants were kept in the imperial elephant stables until around 1900 and were often used for ceremonial occasions, such as the emperor's visits to the Temple of Heaven. Here, however, the large number of horsemen accompanying the emperor's carriage suggests that the emperor was on a much longer journey in the countryside." Paludan, Ann. (1998). Chronicle of the Chinese Emperors: the Reign-by-Reign Record of the Rulers of Imperial China. London: Thames & Hudson Ltd. ISBN 0500050902. Page 177.
image.date: Ming Dynasty, Jiajing Emperor's reign (1522–1566 AD)
image.caption: Departure Herald, a Ming handscroll from the Jiajing reign (1522–1566) showing the emperor's procession leaving Beijing for the imperial tombs.

cities.name: Constantinople
cities.blurb: In Eminönü, Constantinople's busiest commercial quarter, Safiye Sultan, mother of Mehmed III, began a vast mosque in 1597. The Janissaries resented its cost, and work stopped in 1603, leaving it unfinished for decades.

image.file: Ca. 1600 bird's eye view map of Constantinople.jpg
image.description: Ca. 1600 bird's eye view map of Constantinople
image.caption: Bird's-eye view map of Constantinople made around 1600.

cities.name: Agra
cities.blurb: In 1599 Akbar moved the Mughal capital back to Agra from Lahore, returning to the red sandstone fort he had rebuilt in 1565–1573. The English traveller Ralph Fitch had called Agra much greater than London.

image.file: Bau der Festung von Agra (rechte Hälfte).jpg

image.caption: Building the fort at Agra in 1565, an illustration from the Akbarnama painted around 1590 (Victoria and Albert Museum).

cities.name: Osaka
cities.blurb: Toyotomi Hideyoshi completed Osaka Castle, with its gold-leafed main tower, in 1597 and died the next year, leaving it to his son Hideyori. After Sekigahara in 1600 Tokugawa Ieyasu held power; he would besiege the castle in 1614–15.

image.caption: Folding screen of the 1615 summer siege of Osaka Castle, painted in the 17th century for Kuroda Nagamasa.

cities.name: Kyoto
cities.blurb: Home of the imperial court, Kyoto had been remade by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who added north–south streets, gathered temples along Teramachi and ringed the city with earthen odoi walls. In 1601 Tokugawa Ieyasu ordered Nijō Castle built here.

image.caption: Scenes in and around the Capital, a pair of folding screens of Kyoto attributed to Kano Takanobu, Momoyama period (1568–1600).

snapshots.note: Tokugawa Ieyasu's victory at the Battle of Sekigahara in October 1600 made him Japan's paramount warlord; in 1603 he founded the Tokugawa shogunate at Edo.

cities.name: Constantinople
cities.blurb: Constantinople was absorbing the Treaty of Karlowitz of 1699, which ceded large territories to the Habsburgs and Venice. Anger at Sultan Mustafa II's absence in Edirne would fuel the 1703 revolt that deposed him.

image.file: Procession through the Hippodrome, Constantinople (Aubry de La Mottraye's "Travels throughout Europe, Asia and into Part of Africa...," London, 1724, vol. I, plate 15) MET DP824505.jpg

image.caption: A procession through the Hippodrome of Constantinople, a print from Aubry de La Mottraye's Travels, published 1723–24.

cities.name: Edo
cities.blurb: Rebuilt after the Great Fire of Meireki in 1657 with firebreaks and wider streets, the shogun's city had spread east of the Sumida River. It was the prosperous Genroku era, when the arts and architecture flourished.

image.file: Hishikawa Moronobu, Autumn at Asakusa; Viewing Cherry blossoms at Ueno Park, Edo period, Freer Gallery of Art.jpg

cities.name: Beijing
cities.blurb: Qing capital since 1644, Beijing quartered Manchu, Mongol and Han banner troops by the Inner City gates. Northwest of the walls the Kangxi Emperor had built the Changchun Garden in 1684, and would soon begin the Yuanmingyuan.

image.description: The Kangxi-Emperor returns to the Forbidden City after his southern tour in 1689.The imperial court is awaiting the emperors arrival to the palace. Kangxi does not appear in this parts of the roll. The central part is the actual Tian'anmen Square.
image.caption: Detail of the Kangxi Emperor's Southern Inspection Tour scroll (1690s), showing the court awaiting his return to the Forbidden City in 1689.

cities.name: London
cities.blurb: Rebuilt in brick and stone after the Great Fire of 1666, London held the first service in Wren's new St Paul's Cathedral in 1697. By 1700 it handled 80% of England's imports, re-exporting silk, sugar, tea and tobacco.

image.file: City of London Ogilby and Morgan's Map of 1677.jpg

image.caption: Ogilby and Morgan's map of the City of London as rebuilt after the Great Fire, published 1677 (reduced copy).

cities.name: Paris
cities.blurb: Louis XIV had moved the court to Versailles in 1671, yet Paris kept growing: the old walls were demolished to make way for boulevards, and the Place Vendôme was laid out in 1698. Around 1700 London overtook it in size.

image.file: Nicolas de Fer, Huitieme plan de Paris divisé en ses vingts quartiers, 1705.jpg

image.caption: Nicolas de Fer's map of Paris divided into its twenty quarters, published in 1705.

cities.name: Beijing
cities.blurb: In 1750 the Qianlong Emperor began a palace by the Western Lake for his mother's 60th birthday, the future Summer Palace. At the Yuanmingyuan, the Jesuit Giuseppe Castiglione was designing European-style palaces, begun in 1747.

image.file: Beautiful Scene of the Square Pot.jpg
image.description: ​方壺勝景 fāng hú shèng jǐng
image.caption: One of the Forty Scenes of the Yuanmingyuan, an album painted for the Qianlong Emperor by his court painters in 1744.

cities.name: Edo
cities.blurb: Tokugawa Yoshimune's Kyōhō Reforms had reshaped fire-prone Edo: from 1720 townspeople manned 48 iroha fire brigades, and tiled roofs became compulsory. After Yoshimune's death in 1751 the fireproofing drive faltered.

image.file: Large Perspective Picture of Evening Cool by Ryogoku Bridge by Okumura Masanobu.JPG
image.description: Large Perspective Picture of Evening Cool by Ryōgoku Bridge by Okumura Masanobu, early c. 1748, woodblock print with hand-applied lacquer, James Michener Collection, Honolulu Museum of Art accession 21630
image.caption: Evening Cool by Ryōgoku Bridge in Edo, a perspective woodblock print by Okumura Masanobu, about 1748.

cities.name: London
cities.blurb: In 1750 Westminster Bridge opened, the first rival to London Bridge as a Thames crossing, and the Bow Street Runners began as a professional police force. New West End districts such as Mayfair pushed the city beyond its old limits.

image.file: Canaletto - Westminster Bridge, with the Lord Mayor's Procession on the Thames - Google Art Project.jpg
image.caption: Canaletto's Westminster Bridge, with the Lord Mayor's Procession on the Thames, painted in 1747.

cities.name: Constantinople
cities.blurb: Mahmud I, enthroned by the 1730 revolt that ended the Tulip Period, was building the Nuruosmaniye Mosque by the Grand Bazaar: the first sultan's mosque in over a century and the first in the new Ottoman Baroque style.

image.description: Nuruosmaniye Mosque
image.caption: The Nuruosmaniye Mosque, built 1748–1755, photographed in 2018.

cities.name: Paris
cities.blurb: Paris was the hub of the Enlightenment: Diderot and d'Alembert's Encyclopédie began appearing in 1751, and writers met in cafés such as the Procope. Yet Voltaire complained in 1749 that the city centre was dark, cramped and hideous.

image.file: Turgot map of Paris, general map - Norman B. Leventhal Map Center.jpg
image.description: General overview map of the Turgot map of Paris.
image.caption: Overview sheet of the Turgot map of Paris, published in 1739 and showing the city as surveyed in 1734–1736.

cities.name: Beijing
cities.blurb: The Jiaqing Emperor ruled alone after his father Qianlong died in 1799. Beijing had turned away Britain's Macartney embassy, and Anhui opera troupes invited to court in 1790 were starting the blend that became Peking Opera.

image.file: 徐扬京师生春诗意图轴.png
image.caption: Xu Yang's painting of Beijing in spring, Poetic Spring in the Capital, dated 1767.

cities.name: London
cities.blurb: On 12 July 1800 Prime Minister William Pitt helped lay the foundation stone of the West India Docks, London's first commercial wet docks, walled against the theft and delays that plagued the riverside wharves.

image.file: The West India Docks, as they appeared in March 1802 RMG PU1443.jpg
image.description: The West India Docks, as they appeared in March 1802Print by an unknown artist entitled 'West India Docks as they appeared in March 1802', from the 'Gentleman's Magazine', Oct. 1802. It shows the docks as they appeared on completion but before being flooded. Built to put an end to loses suffered from pilfering on the open Thames riverside wharves, the West India Docks stretched for half a mile across the Isle of Dogs. These were the first of the walled docks of the 19th century age of trade. The West India Docks, as they appeared in March 1802
image.caption: The newly completed West India Docks as they appeared in March 1802, a print from the Gentleman's Magazine, October 1802.

cities.name: Guangzhou
cities.blurb: Since 1757 Canton had been the sole legal port for most Western trade with China. European and American traders lived in the Thirteen Factories on the Pearl River, dealing only through the licensed Cohong merchants.

image.file: William Daniell - The European Factories at Canton in China - B1978.43.219 - Yale Center for British Art.jpg
image.caption: William Daniell's painting of the European factories on the waterfront at Canton, 1805.

cities.name: Edo
cities.blurb: Edo was emerging from the Kansei Reforms of 1787–93, launched after famine and the Edo riots of 1787. Matsudaira Sadanobu cut city spending, stockpiled rice and in 1790 enforced Neo-Confucian orthodoxy, banning certain publications.

image.credit: University of British Columbia (UBC Library Digital Collections), https://open.library.ubc.ca/collections/tokugawa/items/1.0216039
image.description: The title is "Famous places of Edo painting", (江戸名所之繪, Edo meisho no e)" [First edition]. Cover attached. This is the first edition; a facsimile of a later edition engraved on another woodblock is reproduced in 日本古地図大成 Nihon kochizu taisei, pl. 77, exposition volume, p. 76. Cited in: WSN; 142.
image.caption: Famous Places of Edo (Edo meisho no e), a pictorial view of the city by Kuwagata Shoshin, first edition 1803.

cities.name: Constantinople
cities.blurb: In 1800 Sultan Selim III built wooden barracks at Üsküdar, on the Asian shore, for the soldiers of his Nizam-ı Cedid, or New Order army. Rebel Janissaries opposed to his reforms burned them in 1806.

image.file: Vue général de Constantinople, prise du chemin de Buyuk Déré - Melling Antoine Ignace - 1819.jpg
image.description: Vue général de Constantinople, prise du chemin de Buyuk Déré - Melling Antoine Ignace - 1819
image.caption: General view of Constantinople from the road to Büyükdere, an engraving after Antoine Ignace Melling, published in 1819.

cities.name: Beijing
cities.blurb: Capital of the Qing emperors, whose Manchu banner garrisons guarded the gates of the Inner City. Opera troupes from Anhui, invited to court since 1790, were laying the foundations of what would become Peking Opera.

image.artist: Great Britain. War Office. Quartermaster-General's Dept
image.credit: National Library of Australia Digital Collection
image.description: Map of the city of Peking (Beijing) in 1817 within the city walls showing towns, streets, fortresses, waterways, palaces and temples of Tseu-Kin Tchhing, Hoang-Tchhing, Nei-Tchhing and Wai-Tchhing. Includes an index to places on left and right panels.
image.caption: Plan of Peking within its walls as it was in 1817, published in 1842.

cities.name: London
cities.polity: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
cities.blurb: In 1825 Marc Brunel began the Thames Tunnel between Rotherhithe and Wapping, dug with his new tunnelling shield to link the docks on both banks. It became the first tunnel successfully built under a navigable river.

image.file: Thames Tunnel,1827, Museum of history and Technology.png
image.description: Projet de Tunnel sous la Tamise, 1827, Museum of history and Technology
image.caption: Print of Brunel's Thames Tunnel project, 1827.

cities.name: Guangzhou
cities.blurb: The only Chinese port open to most Western traders, who were confined to the Thirteen Factories along the Pearl River. Under this Canton System, exports of tea and porcelain made it one of the world's greatest ports.

image.description: View of Foreign Factories, Canton, 1825–1835
image.caption: The foreign factories on the Pearl River at Canton, painted between 1825 and 1835.

cities.name: Paris
cities.blurb: Charles X succeeded his brother Louis XVIII in 1824, and the restored Bourbons were building neoclassical churches to replace those lost in the Revolution. The Canal Saint-Martin, bringing fresh water from the Ourcq, was completed in 1825.

image.credit: Potier, Baptiste - La Rotonde de la Villette, histoire d'un catalyseur urbain. Paris, 2011. Vol II. Annexes p.67.
image.caption: The Barrière Saint-Martin and the basin of the Ourcq canal, coloured etching, about 1820.

cities.name: Edo
cities.blurb: Seat of the Tokugawa shoguns, while the emperor remained in Kyoto. Its book trade was booming, with more than 800 booksellers by the 1830s, and artists such as Hokusai and Hiroshige were depicting its streets.

image.file: 冨嶽三十六景 江戸日本橋-Nihonbashi in Edo (Edo Nihonbashi), from the series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji (Fugaku sanjūrokkei) MET DP141003.jpg

cities.name: London
cities.polity: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
cities.blurb: King's Cross, the latest of the great railway termini, opened in 1850. The next year the Great Exhibition in Hyde Park's Crystal Palace drew six million visitors and displayed Britain at the height of its imperial dominance.

image.file: Crystal Palace from the northeast from Dickinson's Comprehensive Pictures of the Great Exhibition of 1851. 1854.jpg
image.credit: Dickinsons' comprehensive pictures of the Great Exhibition of 1851
image.description: The Crystal Palace from the northeast during the Great Exhibition of 1851.
image.caption: The Crystal Palace in Hyde Park during the Great Exhibition of 1851, from Dickinson's Comprehensive Pictures (1854).

cities.name: Beijing
cities.blurb: The 19-year-old Xianfeng Emperor took the throne in 1850, inheriting an empire in crisis. That December the Taiping Rebellion broke out in the south, and the Nian rebels' cavalry would soon threaten the capital itself.

image.file: Felice Beato (British, born Italy - Top of the Wall of Peking - Google Art Project.jpg
image.credit: 8gFawUPc3Elzsg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level
image.caption: Felice Beato's photograph from the top of Peking's city wall, October 1860, among the earliest photographs of the city.

cities.name: Paris
cities.blurb: Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte, elected president in 1848, ruled a crowded, unhealthy city where cholera had killed twenty thousand that year. He seized power in 1851, and his rebuilding of Paris with Haussmann began in 1853.

image.file: Charles Marville, Rue Tirechape, de la rue de Rivoli, ca. 1853–70, edited.jpg

image.caption: Charles Marville's photograph of the narrow Rue Tirechape in old central Paris, taken between about 1853 and 1870.

cities.name: Guangzhou
cities.blurb: The 1842 Treaty of Nanking ended the Canton System, and trade was shifting to new treaty ports. The foreign factories, burned in the First Opium War, had been rebuilt, while local viceroys resisted opening the walled city to foreigners.

image.description: Canton (Guangzhou), Die Hongs oder die ausländischen Factoreien am Perlfluß in Canton. Gouache auf Velin, um 1850
image.caption: Gouache of the hongs, the foreign factories on the Pearl River at Canton, about 1850.

cities.name: Constantinople
cities.blurb: Capital of the Ottoman Empire in the era of the Tanzimat reforms, which brought new technology and bridges across the Golden Horn. Sultan Abdülmecid I was building the European-style Dolmabahçe Palace on the Bosphorus to replace medieval Topkapı.

image.file: Robertson & Beato - Dolmabahçe Palace and Mosque - Google Art Project.jpg
image.artist: Robertson & Beato (1813 - 1888) (British) Born in Middlesex, England. Died in Japan. Details on Google Art Project
image.credit: OAGvc_x9NAWOsw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level
image.caption: Dolmabahçe Palace and Mosque on the Bosphorus, photographed by Robertson & Beato in the mid-19th century.

snapshots.note: Industrialisation was drawing huge numbers of rural migrants into cities, first in Europe. London's population had more than doubled since 1800, making it by far the world's largest city.

cities.name: London
cities.polity: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
cities.blurb: Joseph Bazalgette's vast sewer network, begun after the Great Stink of 1858, was cleaning up the Thames. The Underground, open since 1863, and new metropolitan railways let middle-class Londoners commute from spreading suburbs.

image.description: Adolphe François Pannemaker (b. 1822) after Gustave Doré (1832–1883), "Over London – by Rail", from London: A Pilgrimage (London: Grant & Co., 1872), engraving, Yale Center for British Art, Paul Mellon Collection
image.caption: Gustave Doré's engraving 'Over London - by Rail', from London: A Pilgrimage (1872).

cities.name: Paris
cities.blurb: Recovering from the 1871 Commune, whose fighters burned the Tuileries Palace and the Hôtel de Ville. The Palais Garnier opera house, begun under Napoleon III, was completed in 1875, and the Hôtel de Ville was being rebuilt.

image.file: Inauguration of the Paris Opera in 1875 by Detaille - Collections of the Château of Versailles (cropped).jpg

image.caption: Édouard Detaille's gouache of the inauguration of the Paris Opera on 5 January 1875, painted in 1878.

cities.name: New York
cities.blurb: Its harbour handled most American exports, and Boss Tweed had been convicted in 1873 of defrauding the city. Across the East River, the Brooklyn Bridge's towers were rising to link Manhattan with the separate city of Brooklyn.

sources.title: History of New York City (1855–1897) - Wikipedia
History of New York City (1855–1897) - Wikipedia

cities.name: Berlin
cities.blurb: Capital of the new German Empire since 1871, with its bureaucracy and military expanding fast. Sanitation was among the worst in Europe, and a modern sewer system was built in the late 1870s.

image.credit: Collection of the Technical University of Berlin Scanned from Janos Frecot & Helmut Geisert: Berlin in frühen Photographien 1857–1913. Schirmer/Mosel, Munich 1984. ISBN 3-88814-984-3.
image.description: The Kaisergalerie (“Emperor Galery”) in Berlin's Friedrichstraße, on the corner to Behrenstraße. The building opened in 1873. It was largely destroyed in 1943 by an allied air raid. The place now holds the hotel Westin Grand Berlin.
image.caption: The Kaisergalerie shopping arcade on Friedrichstraße, opened in 1873, photographed around 1875.

cities.name: Vienna
cities.blurb: The Ringstraße, a grand boulevard lined with palaces, had replaced the old city walls. The 1873 World's Fair in the Prater marked Franz Joseph's 25 years as emperor, but a cholera outbreak and a stock-market crash kept visitors away.

image.credit: Welt ausstellen. Schauplatz Wien 1873. Herausgeber Technisches Museum Wien, ISBN 3-902183-10-1
image.description: Main Entrance of the Rotunde with topping-out decoration, Expo 1873
image.caption: Main entrance of the Rotunde, the centrepiece of the 1873 Vienna World's Fair, photographed in 1873.

cities.name: London
cities.polity: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
cities.blurb: At the height of its influence as capital of one of history's largest empires. The London County Council, created in 1888, governed the capital, and in 1900 its county was divided into 28 metropolitan boroughs.

image.description: Cheapside, London, England 1 photomechanical print : photochrom, color.
image.caption: Photochrom print of busy Cheapside in the City of London, made between 1890 and 1900.

cities.name: New York
cities.blurb: Consolidated in 1898 from Manhattan, Brooklyn, the Bronx, Queens and Staten Island. Its first subway line, opened in 1904, would help bind the five boroughs together, while early skyscrapers rose in Manhattan.

sources.title: History of New York City (1898–1945) - Wikipedia

image.description: Columbus Circle during construction of the New York City Subway in 1900.
image.caption: Columbus Circle dug up for construction of the New York City Subway, March 1900.

cities.name: Paris
cities.blurb: The Exposition Universelle drew fifty million visitors and popularised Art Nouveau worldwide, and the first Métro line opened in time for it. The Grand Palais and Petit Palais were built for the fair.

image.file: Grand entrance, Exposition Universal, 1900, Paris, France.jpg

image.caption: The monumental main entrance of the 1900 Exposition Universelle, photographed in 1900.

cities.name: Berlin
cities.blurb: An industrial city whose electrical-machinery industry had boomed since the 1880s. Work on the U-Bahn had begun in 1896, and tenement blocks were filling Kreuzberg, Prenzlauer Berg, Friedrichshain and Wedding.

image.credit: This image is available from the United States Library of Congress's Prints and Photographs division under the digital ID ppmsca.00347.This tag does not indicate the copyright status of the attached work. A normal copyright tag is still required. See Commons:Licensing.

On the far right, one of Karl Schinkel's Doric temples (part of the former Potsdam Gate), can be seen at the entrance to Leipziger Platz.
image.caption: Potsdamer Platz, flanked by the Grand Hotel Belle Vue and the Palast Hotel, around 1900.

cities.name: Chicago
cities.blurb: In 1900 the new Sanitary and Ship Canal reversed the Chicago River to carry sewage away from Lake Michigan. The nation's railroad hub had hosted the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, and most residents were immigrants or their children.

sources.title: Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal - Wikipedia

cities.name: New York
cities.blurb: Harlem, the political capital of Black America, was the heart of the Harlem Renaissance, home to writers such as Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston. Skyscrapers were transforming the skyline as housing spread across Queens and outer Brooklyn.

sources.title: History of New York City (1898–1945) - Wikipedia
History of New York City (1898–1945) - Wikipedia

image.caption: Guests at a breakfast party for Langston Hughes at 580 St. Nicholas Avenue, Harlem, May 1925.

cities.name: London
cities.blurb: The British Empire Exhibition at Wembley, open in 1924 and 1925, aimed to strengthen imperial bonds and trade. Suburbs of semi-detached houses were spreading beyond the County of London into Middlesex, Essex, Hertfordshire, Kent and Surrey.

image.description: Postcard depicting the Wembley Stadium in London.
image.caption: Postcard of Wembley Stadium at the British Empire Exhibition, 1924.

cities.name: Tokyo
cities.blurb: Rebuilding after the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake and the fires that followed. Concrete buildings had survived best, spurring a shift to earthquake-proof construction, and the first underground railway outside Europe and the Americas would open in 1927.

image.file: Groundbreaking ceremony of Tokyo Underground Railway 1.jpg

image.caption: Groundbreaking ceremony for the Tokyo Underground Railway's Ueno-Asakusa line, today's Ginza Line, 27 September 1925.

cities.name: Paris
cities.blurb: In les années folles, artists and writers from around the world gathered in Montparnasse cafés, and the 1925 International Exhibition of Modern Decorative and Industrial Arts gave Art Deco its name. The old fortifications were being torn down.

sources.title: International Exhibition of Modern Decorative and Industrial Arts - Wikipedia

image.caption: The 1925 International Exhibition of Modern Decorative and Industrial Arts on the Esplanade des Invalides, July 1925.

cities.name: Berlin
cities.blurb: Enlarged by the 1920 Greater Berlin Act and stabilised after the 1923 hyperinflation, it was continental Europe's largest industrial city. The Golden Twenties brought booming nightlife, the new S-Bahn and Tempelhof airport.

image.credit: Franziska Nentwig (Hg.): Berlin im Licht, Berlin 2008, S. 159
image.description: Potsdamer Platz, Berlin
image.caption: Max Missmann's photograph of traffic on Potsdamer Platz, 1925.

snapshots.note: In the interwar years cars, electric lighting and radio became common in the richest countries, and the Roaring Twenties preceded the Great Depression. In the early 1920s New York overtook London as the world's most populous urban area.

cities.name: New York
cities.blurb: With many great cities in ruins after the war, New York took on new global prominence. The United Nations headquarters was rising beside the East River, and abstract expressionism was making the city the centre of the art world.

sources.title: History of New York City (1946–1977) - Wikipedia
Headquarters of the United Nations - Wikipedia

cities.name: Tokyo
cities.blurb: Still under American occupation, with General MacArthur's headquarters in Marunouchi. Governed since 1943 as the Tokyo Metropolis, the bomb-damaged city would use profits from the Korean War, which began in 1950, for rebuilding.

cities.name: London
cities.blurb: Rebuilding was slow after so much housing was destroyed in the war, and the authorities were turning to high-rise flats to ease the shortage. The 1951 Festival of Britain on the South Bank would mark a new mood of optimism.

image.description: Festival of Britain Exhibition, South Bank, London 1951. Dome of Discovery to left, Skylon centre and Transport Pavilion to right. In the distance, across the River Thames, the building of the National Liberal Club is visible.
image.caption: The Festival of Britain on the South Bank in July 1951, with the Dome of Discovery and the Skylon.

cities.name: Osaka
cities.blurb: The UN figure covers the wider Keihanshin region, including Kyoto and Kobe. American B-29 raids in 1945 had devastated large parts of Osaka, and the rebuilding of its factories and trade was under way.

image.description: Caption: April 26, 1950. Busy street scene near the Osaka central depot. Citation: Mennonite Community Photographs, 1947-1953: Service. HM4-134 Box 1 Photo 030-19. Mennonite Church USA Archives - Goshen. Goshen, Indiana.
image.caption: Busy street near Osaka's central station, 26 April 1950.

cities.name: Paris
cities.blurb: Bread rationing had ended only in 1948, and most apartments lacked their own bathroom. In 1950 the government began building HLM low-rent housing on the city's edges, while strikes and Communist-led protests kept politics turbulent.

image.credit: Stockholm Transport Museum Commons - Photo Nr: 2219-B549
image.description: Un bus à plate-forme Renault TN de la ligne 168 à la porte de Clignancourt à Paris.
image.caption: A Renault TN platform bus on route 168 at the Porte de Clignancourt, 1950.

snapshots.note: From 1950, sizes come from the UN's World Urbanization Prospects, which counts urban agglomerations: a city plus its surrounding built-up area, regardless of administrative boundaries. Earlier years use historians' estimates, so part of the jump reflects this change.

cities.name: Tokyo
cities.blurb: Tokyo was spending heavily on infrastructure for the 1964 Summer Olympics: the Toei Subway opened its first line in 1960, and the Tōkaidō Shinkansen to Osaka, the world's first high-speed railway, opened in time for the Games.

image.description: Tokyo Olympics 1964 Opening Ceremony.
image.caption: Opening ceremony of the Tokyo Summer Olympics, photographed 10 October 1964.

cities.name: New York
cities.blurb: Urban renewal reached Lower Manhattan around 1960 with One Chase Manhattan Plaza, while Robert Moses's highways cut through neighbourhoods; the demolition of Pennsylvania Station led to the city's 1965 landmarks preservation law.

sources.title: History of New York City (1946–1977) - Wikipedia

cities.name: Osaka
cities.blurb: Rebuilt factories and revived trade were making Osaka prosperous, and growth spilled into the suburbs; the Tōkaidō Shinkansen, begun in 1959, opened in 1964 and linked Shin-Ōsaka with Tokyo in four hours.

image.description: Aerial photograph around Shin-Osaka Station (May 1964)
image.caption: Aerial photograph of the area around the new Shin-Ōsaka Station, May 1964.

cities.name: London
cities.blurb: Tower blocks were rising across London to replace war-damaged housing, and in 1965 the new Greater London Council took over a much larger area; by the mid-1960s Carnaby Street was the emblem of Swinging London.

image.credit: This file is from the collections of The National Archives (United Kingdom), catalogued under document record INF14/147. For high quality reproductions of any item from The National Archives collection please contact the image library.

image.caption: Young people on Carnaby Street, the heart of Swinging London, around 1966.

cities.name: Paris
cities.blurb: Under de Gaulle's new Fifth Republic, Paris saw bombings and deadly clashes over Algerian independence in 1961–62; the government built a market at Rungis to replace Les Halles and had soot cleaned from Notre-Dame.

image.artist: Roger Wollstadt from Sarasota, Florida, U.S.A.

image.caption: Les Halles, the old central market of Paris, photographed 11 May 1960.

cities.name: Tokyo
cities.blurb: With the old 30-metre height limit lifted, skyscrapers arrived: the Kasumigaseki Building opened in 1968 and the Keio Plaza Hotel rose in west Shinjuku. Tama New Town opened in 1971, and the 1973 oil crisis brought inflation.

image.description: 842b Ginza, Tokyo, Japan 1971
image.caption: Ginza, Tokyo, photographed in 1971.

cities.name: New York
cities.blurb: The World Trade Center's Twin Towers opened in 1972, a rare high point as residents and industry left; in 1975 the city ran out of money and only narrowly avoided defaulting on its debts.

cities.name: Mexico City
cities.blurb: The 1968 Olympics, preceded by government troops' massacre of protesting students at Tlatelolco, were followed in 1969 by the first Metro line; through the 1970s smog and shanty towns grew faster than services.

image.caption: Students on a burned bus during the protests in Mexico City, July 1968.

cities.name: Buenos Aires
cities.blurb: The city was torn by fighting between left-wing guerrillas and the right-wing Triple A; after the 1976 coup, the Dirty War's disappearances brought the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo to march silently.
